promptText: What does a container actually virtualize, and why does that make it faster to start than a virtual machine?
options: It virtualizes the operating system by isolating a process on the shared host kernel, so there is no separate OS to boot
It virtualizes the physical hardware exactly like a VM, just with a smaller disk image
It virtualizes only the network stack while running a full guest OS underneath
It virtualizes the CPU instruction set, which removes the need for a kernel entirely
explanation: A container is an isolated process sharing the host kernel rather than a full OS per instance, which is why it starts in milliseconds and uses a fraction of the memory a VM needs - VMs virtualize hardware, containers virtualize the operating system.

promptText: Using the class/object analogy from the chapter, what is the relationship between a Docker image and a Docker container?
options: An image is the immutable, versioned template (the class); a container is a running instance of it (the object)
An image and a container are two names for the same artifact used interchangeably
A container is the template stored in a registry; an image is the running process
An image can only ever produce exactly one container before it must be rebuilt
explanation: The image is a read-only template built from a Dockerfile, and many containers can be started from that one image, just as many objects can be created from one class - containers are ephemeral and disposable while images are immutable and versioned by tag.

promptText: If a pod's readiness probe starts failing, what does Kubernetes do?
options: It stops routing traffic to that pod but does not restart the container
It immediately restarts the container to try to recover it
It deletes the pod and creates a completely new Deployment
It marks the entire node as unschedulable
explanation: Readiness answers 'should this receive traffic right now?' - a failing readiness probe only removes the pod from the Service's routing until it passes again, whereas a failing liveness probe is what triggers a restart; confusing the two causes restart loops or traffic sent to a not-yet-ready app.

promptText: Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted by default when stored?
options: No, they are only base64-encoded by default; encryption at rest and/or an external vault must be added deliberately
Yes, Secrets are always AES-256 encrypted automatically with no configuration needed
Secrets are stored in plaintext but only readable by the pod's own ServiceAccount
Secrets are encrypted only when created through a ConfigMap reference
explanation: A common gap candidates miss: Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted, by default - production setups must enable encryption-at-rest and often integrate an external vault such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager for real protection.

promptText: Which deployment strategy is the right fit for a high-risk change where you want to validate against real production traffic before committing fully, while limiting the blast radius of a bad release?
options: Canary - send a small percentage of traffic to the new version and ramp up gradually
Blue-green - run two full environments and switch all traffic at once
Rolling - gradually replace old pods with new ones with no traffic-percentage control
Recreate - terminate all old pods before starting any new ones
explanation: Canary limits blast radius by exposing the new version to a small slice of real users first and watching metrics before a full rollout, which is exactly the trade-off you want for a high-risk change; blue-green gives an instant cutover but no gradual real-traffic validation.

promptText: What does the 12-factor 'config in the environment' principle enable in practice?
options: The same immutable image can run unchanged in dev, staging and production, differing only by injected configuration
Every environment must build and maintain its own separate Docker image
Configuration values must be compiled directly into the application's source code
Environment variables are only used for logging verbosity settings
explanation: Never hard-coding environment-specific values into the build and instead injecting them at runtime is what lets you 'build once, deploy anywhere' - Spring profiles and application.yml overridden by environment variables are this principle applied directly.

promptText: Why does copying the dependency descriptor (e.g. pom.xml) and downloading dependencies BEFORE copying application source code speed up Docker rebuilds?
options: Docker reuses cached layers up to the first changed instruction, so a source-only change reuses the already-cached dependency layer instead of re-downloading everything
Maven requires the pom.xml to be present before any other file can be copied into an image
It reduces the final image size by excluding the dependency cache from the runtime layer
Docker automatically parallelizes any COPY instruction that appears before source code
explanation: Each instruction creates a cached layer, and a rebuild reuses layers up to the first instruction that changed; ordering the rarely-changing dependency download before the frequently-changing source copy means a typical code change only invalidates the layers after it, not the expensive dependency download.

promptText: A team writes a secret to a file in one RUN instruction and deletes it in a later RUN instruction within the same Dockerfile, assuming this keeps the final image clean. Why is this still a security problem?
options: Docker layers are additive and immutable, so the secret still exists in the earlier layer's diff and can be extracted with tools like docker history even though it's hidden from the final filesystem view
Docker automatically scans and blocks any RUN command that references the word 'secret'
Deleting a file in a later layer causes the build to fail rather than succeed silently
The secret is only a problem if the image is pushed to a public registry, not a private one
explanation: Because layers are additive and immutable, a later layer's deletion only hides the file in the final merged view - it does not remove it from the image's history, so the secret remains recoverable; this is exactly why BuildKit's --mount=type=secret and multi-stage builds exist.

promptText: A JVM's -Xmx is set almost equal to the container's memory limit, yet the container still gets OOMKilled under load. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The JVM's total footprint includes metaspace, thread stacks and native buffers beyond the heap, and that non-heap memory pushed the cgroup past its limit
OOMKilled only ever happens due to CPU throttling, never actual memory pressure
Setting -Xmx close to the container limit always causes an immediate crash on startup, not under load
The container limit only applies to disk I/O, not memory, so this scenario is not related to the limit
explanation: Container memory limits are a hard cgroup boundary covering the whole process, not just JVM heap - metaspace, thread stacks and native/off-heap buffers all count too, so a heap sized right up to the limit still leaves the process vulnerable to OOMKilled from non-heap memory pressure.

promptText: Why is a Kubernetes rollback typically fast, rather than requiring a full redeploy from scratch?
options: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, not Pods directly, so rolling back just scales the previous (already-known) ReplicaSet back up while scaling the current one down
Kubernetes caches the entire application state in etcd and can restore it instantly without touching any pods
Rollback only changes a label on existing pods rather than creating or destroying any resources
kubectl rollout undo re-pulls the previous image from the registry in parallel across all nodes
explanation: Kubernetes never edits pods in place - a Deployment change creates a new ReplicaSet, and old ReplicaSets are kept scaled to zero (up to revisionHistoryLimit); a rollback is just the same surge/drain mechanism as a forward rollout, pointed backwards at an already-defined ReplicaSet.

promptText: Why do clustered stateful systems like Kafka or a self-hosted Postgres primary/replica set typically need a StatefulSet with ordered creation, rather than a Deployment?
options: Cluster formation and leader election often require pods to come up in a known order with stable identity and dedicated storage that follows a specific pod across rescheduling
StatefulSets are simply a newer API version of Deployment with no functional difference
Deployments cannot attach any persistent volume to a pod under any circumstance
StatefulSets automatically replicate data between pods without any application-level configuration
explanation: A Deployment's pods are interchangeable with no ordering guarantee, but a StatefulSet gives each replica a stable name, stable DNS, and its own persistent volume via a volumeClaimTemplate, and defaults to ordered one-at-a-time creation - exactly what many stateful systems need for cluster formation.

promptText: Why can't a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler function on a Deployment whose pods have no CPU request configured?
options: HPA computes utilization as a percentage of the configured CPU request, so with no request there is no baseline to calculate a percentage against
HPA requires a minimum of three replicas before it can begin evaluating any metric at all
HPA only reads memory usage and never considers CPU regardless of configuration
Requests are only used by the scheduler and have no relationship to autoscaling metrics
explanation: The HPA's target (e.g. 70% CPU utilization) is meaningless without a request to measure against - '70% of what request' has no answer if none is set, so a pod with no CPU request configured makes the HPA unable to compute a desired replica count.

promptText: A Deployment's rolling update is configured with maxSurge: 25% and maxUnavailable: 25%, but the new version's readiness probe never passes. What actually happens, and what is required to recover?
options: The rollout stalls partway through - it does not automatically roll back - so a human or automation must observe kubectl rollout status and run kubectl rollout undo
Kubernetes automatically reverts to the previous ReplicaSet within seconds once it detects the probe failing repeatedly
The rollout completes anyway since maxUnavailable guarantees full traffic capacity regardless of pod health
The old ReplicaSet is deleted immediately, causing a full outage until the new version's probe passes
explanation: maxSurge/maxUnavailable govern the pace and availability budget of a rolling update, but the default rolling update only guarantees availability during the process, not correctness of the new version - if readiness never passes, progress stalls at whatever point it reached and someone must issue rollout undo.

promptText: One pod sets requests equal to limits for both CPU and memory (Guaranteed QoS). A second pod on the same node sets no requests or limits at all (BestEffort). Under sudden node memory pressure, which pod does the kubelet evict first, and why?
options: The BestEffort pod, because Kubernetes evicts pods in QoS order - BestEffort first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed last
The Guaranteed pod, because it is consuming a fixed, predictable amount of memory that is easier to reclaim
Both pods are evicted simultaneously since QoS class has no bearing on eviction order
Neither pod is evicted; only pods exceeding their own limit can ever be evicted under memory pressure
explanation: QoS class is derived automatically from how requests/limits are set, and the kubelet evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed last under node memory pressure - this is why anything that must not be evicted (a database, a payment service) should set requests equal to limits.

promptText: A team adds a single NetworkPolicy that allows ingress to the order-service pods only from the api-gateway pods on port 8080. Afterward, order-service can no longer reach an unrelated database it also depends on. What explains this, and what fixes it?
options: Once a pod is selected by any NetworkPolicy for a direction, that direction becomes default-deny except for what is explicitly allowed - a separate egress rule must be added for the database traffic
NetworkPolicies only ever affect ingress traffic, so this outage must be caused by something unrelated to the new policy
NetworkPolicies are purely advisory unless RBAC is also configured, so the outage is actually an RBAC misconfiguration
The policy accidentally blocked all traffic cluster-wide because NetworkPolicies apply globally rather than being scoped by pod selector
explanation: The policy only declared an ingress rule, but Kubernetes networking is flat and open by default; being selected by any NetworkPolicy flips a pod's matching direction to default-deny except for explicitly allowed traffic - if the outbound database connection wasn't covered by an egress rule, it silently stops working, a well-known cause of unexpected outages.
